summary:
We built CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, an interactive web app that helps people explore how location and timing affect a mission on the Moon. Users can choose a lunar site or enter their own coordinates, select a date and time, and see where the Sun and Earth would appear above the local horizon in 3D. Using NASA/JPL Horizons data, the app also lets users follow their movement over time, compare scenarios side by side, and explore estimated solar power and direct-to-Earth communication under adjustable mission assumptions.

Our project addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by bringing this information into one clear, accessible interface, available in English and Spanish. Instead of working through tables of numbers, users can see what changes when they move to another site or shift a mission date.

These differences matter: a mission needs power and a way to communicate with Earth. Our tool helps users understand those constraints and explore alternatives, while making its limits clear: it does not model terrain or guarantee that a landing site is suitable.
details:
https://github.com/saam-rk/larping-masters-space-apps

What we built

CLPS Lunar Mission Browser is an interactive web app for exploring possible lunar landing sites and dates. It focuses on two practical questions: where will the Sun be, and where will the Earth be? Their positions help us understand the possibilities for solar power and direct communication with Earth.

Users can choose a reference site or enter custom lunar coordinates, select a date and time, and explore a 3D view of the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon. The app retrieves their positions from NASA/JPL Horizons and shows the readings alongside the visualisation, with sources, units and explanations.

How it works

The app lets users explore one moment or play through a time interval to see how the positions change. They can also compare up to four location-and-date scenarios side by side. This makes it easier to explore questions such as: “What changes if we arrive a week later?” or “How different are the conditions at another site?”

For users who want more detail, an advanced mode includes:

  • A search for times when the Sun or Earth is within a chosen part of the sky.
  • Solar power estimates based on adjustable panel size, efficiency, orientation and power demand.
  • A simplified direct-to-Earth communication assessment based on user-entered radio settings.
  • An overview of how those conditions change over roughly one lunar month.

Why it matters

Choosing a lunar landing site is not just about picking a point on a map. Timing also matters, and a change in schedule can change the conditions a mission would face.

Our goal is to make those relationships easier to understand without asking users to work through raw astronomical tables. The app can support early exploration of mission options and help students, educators and curious users understand some of the challenges of operating on the Moon. It is available in Spanish and English.

Tools and development

We built the app with TypeScript and React, using React Three Fiber and Three.js for the interactive 3D views, and Vite for development and production builds. A server-side API connects the app to NASA/JPL Horizons, and the backend is structured for Vercel Functions. We also developed automated tests for calculations, data handling and interface behaviour.

Our approach and design choices

The creative part of our project is bringing visual exploration, time playback, scenario comparison and adjustable mission assumptions into one experience. Users can start with a simple view and open the advanced tools when they need them.

We considered ease of use, different levels of scientific knowledge, traceable data and honest communication of uncertainty. Missing data is shown as unknown rather than treated as zero, and saved demonstration data is distinguished from live results.

We also separate what the visualisation shows from what the calculations can establish. Local terrain is not included in the power and communication assessments, so mountains and craters may change real conditions. Our results are a starting point for comparing options—not a guarantee of power, communication or a suitable landing site.
